steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to a known-good AC power source and observe startup behavior to determine whether TF 5510 remains present or returns after the device begins operating.

steps.title: Check Accessible Cable and Connection Condition
steps.instructions: Inspect permitted accessible cabling and connections associated with the autozero valve and connector board area for looseness, strain, contamination, corrosion, or signs of prior service disturbance. Reseat only accessible connections when authorized by procedure and service documentation.

steps.title: Recheck for Error TF 5510
steps.instructions: After any permitted accessible correction, restart the ventilator and review the event log for a new occurrence. If TF 5510 returns, stop at the external-check level and escalate for bench evaluation or authorized repair.

steps.title: Stop When Resolved
steps.instructions: Return the ventilator to service only after the error no longer occurs, no new fault is recorded, and all required functional and safety checks pass according to department procedure.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed Error TF 5510 during operation. Technical fault indicated elevated dP Sensor signal consistent with suspected autozero valve switching failure. Ventilation continued while fault was displayed.
CCR.Cause: Confirmed recurrent TF 5510 in the event log. Inspected external condition and accessible connection path associated with the autozero valve and connector board circuit. No correctable external issue identified; fault is consistent with suspected internal autozero valve circuit, connector board, or sensor board failure.
CCR.Resolution: Removed ventilator from clinical service, labeled unit Out of Service, and routed for bench evaluation or authorized repair. Alternative ventilation was required before troubleshooting because the ventilator reported an unresolved technical fault during operation.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 5511 dP Flow Sensor Signal Out of Range During Autozeroing
description: Troubleshooting TF 5511 when the dP flow sensor signal is out of range during autozeroing, potentially affecting dependable ventilator flow measurement.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the Hamilton G5 is connected to a patient, notify clinical staff and arrange an approved alternative ventilator before removing the device from use. Do not rely on a ventilator with an unresolved flow-sensor-related technical fault, even if ventilation continues.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm that Error: TF 5511 is displayed or recorded in the event log. Document whether the error occurred during startup, an autozero cycle, intermittent operation, movement, cleaning, or recent service, and note additional alarms or abnormal flow readings.

steps.title: Inspect the Ventilator for External Damage or Contamination
steps.instructions: With the device removed from patient use, inspect accessible external areas for visible damage, fluid intrusion, contamination, signs of impact, or damaged accessories. Do not open the device during initial troubleshooting.

steps.title: Rule Out Accessory and Setup-Related Concerns
steps.instructions: Confirm that the breathing circuit and user-accessible flow-related accessories are installed correctly, appropriate for the device configuration, and free of obvious damage or obstruction. Document accessories connected when the error occurred.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: Confirm the occurrence, date, time, recurrence, and any related technical faults associated with TF 5511 according to facility-approved procedures.

steps.title: Evaluate Whether the Error Clears After Safe Restart Testing
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from patient use and connected to appropriate test equipment or a test circuit, perform controlled restart testing and observe for repeated TF 5511 faults or abnormal behavior.

steps.title: Isolate as an Internal Device Fault When External Causes Are Ruled Out
steps.instructions: If TF 5511 persists or recurs after external checks and controlled testing, remove the unit from service and route it for qualified bench evaluation of the autozero valve signal path, associated cabling, connector board, or sensor board as indicated.

steps.title: Stop When Resolved
steps.instructions: Return the ventilator to service only if a correctable external condition was addressed and appropriate operational verification shows no repeated TF 5511 fault. If the error recurs or cannot be confidently resolved, keep the device out of service.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed Error: TF 5511 during startup or operation. Device continued ventilation, but the technical fault indicated the dP flow sensor signal was outside acceptable range during autozeroing.
CCR.Cause: Verified TF 5511 in the event log. External inspection and accessory/setup checks did not identify a correctable external cause. Repeated fault indicates likely internal autozero valve signal path, cabling, connector board, or sensor board issue.
CCR.Resolution: Removed ventilator from clinical service, labeled unit Out of Service, documented event log findings, and routed device for qualified bench evaluation and repair of the autozero valve/flow sensor signal circuit as indicated.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 5512 Paw Pressure Sensor Autozero Out of Range
description: Troubleshooting TF 5512 when the Paw pressure sensor is outside its allowable range during autozeroing, allowing ventilation to continue while potentially affecting reliable airway pressure sensing.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the ventilator is connected to a patient, notify clinical staff and provide alternative ventilation before troubleshooting. Do not continue relying on a ventilator reporting a suspected airway pressure sensing fault.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 5512 on the display or in the event log. Document when the error occurs, whether ventilation continues, and whether additional pressure, flow, or technical faults are present.

steps.title: Inspect the Ventilator for External Problems
steps.instructions: Inspect the ventilator for physical damage, liquid intrusion, contamination, damaged circuit connections, or obstruction of pressure-related ports. Do not introduce fluids or probes into device ports.

steps.title: Check the Breathing Circuit and External Accessories
steps.instructions: Inspect tubing, circuit components, flow sensor components, water accumulation, connections, and accessory compatibility. Replace questionable external components with known-good compatible accessories before retesting.

steps.title: Confirm Proper Power and Test Setup
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to stable AC power, remove it from patient use, install required test accessories, and prepare the unit for controlled Test Mode evaluation according to facility procedure.

steps.title: Perform Pressure Sensor Zero Calibrations in Test Mode
steps.instructions: Perform the approved pressure sensor zero calibrations in Test Mode. Determine whether calibration completes, whether TF 5512 clears, and whether additional pressure or autozero faults appear.

steps.title: Review the Event Log and Determine Final Device Status
steps.instructions: Document TF 5512 history, calibration results, related faults, recurrence after restart or testing, and final equipment disposition. Escalate persistent faults for authorized bench repair.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed Error: TF 5512 during autozeroing. Ventilation continued, but the technical fault indicated the Paw pressure sensor zero reading was outside allowable range.
CCR.Cause: Confirmed recurring TF 5512 during non-clinical testing. External inspection and circuit/accessory checks revealed no contributing issue. Pressure sensor zero calibration did not clear the fault, indicating likely internal Paw pressure sensing or autozero system failure.
CCR.Resolution: Removed ventilator from service and labeled Out of Service. Documented event log findings and calibration results. Referred unit for authorized bench evaluation of the Paw pressure sensing and autozero system.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 5513 Error Fan Signal Active
description: Troubleshooting TF 5513 when abnormal cooling fan operation causes a high-priority technical fault and may place the ventilator at risk of overheating or later failure.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Notify clinical staff and provide alternative ventilation or transfer the patient to a known-working ventilator before troubleshooting TF 5513. Do not rely on continued ventilation from a device displaying an unresolved high-priority cooling-fan technical fault.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 5513 is displayed, determine whether it occurred during startup or ventilation, document whether it is continuous or intermittent, identify any associated technical faults, and review the event log.

steps.title: Check the Device Exterior for Cooling Obstruction
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from patient use, inspect external cooling intake and exhaust openings for dust, debris, contamination, blocked airflow, unusual heat, odor, or abnormal noise. Remove only external obstructions according to approved practices.

steps.title: Confirm Power and Operating Environment
steps.instructions: Verify stable approved power, check for power interruptions associated with the fault, and confirm the ventilator is not exposed to excessive heat or positioned where normal cooling airflow is restricted.

steps.title: Observe Error Recurrence During a Controlled Bench Check
steps.instructions: In a controlled bench setting, observe whether TF 5513 returns and listen for grinding, clicking, scraping, vibration, or abnormal fan behavior. Review the event log again and do not return the ventilator to use solely because the error clears temporarily.

steps.title: Recheck After Correcting an External Issue
steps.instructions: If an external airflow or environmental issue was corrected, restart the ventilator in a controlled bench setting, monitor for recurrence, review the event log, and complete applicable functional and safety checks before any return-to-service decision.

steps.title: Isolate a Likely Device-Related Fan Failure
steps.instructions: If TF 5513 persists after external conditions have been ruled out, remove the device from service, document the fault, and refer it for qualified evaluation of the fan assembly, fan connection, or associated servo/inspiratory module circuitry.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed high-priority technical fault TF 5513 Error Fan Signal Active during operation. Ventilation continued, but the unit was removed from patient use due to possible cooling fan failure.
CCR.Cause: Event log confirmed TF 5513. External cooling openings and operating environment were inspected with no airflow restriction identified. Fault recurred during controlled bench observation, indicating a likely internal fan assembly or associated module fault.
CCR.Resolution: Recommended alternative ventilation, removed ventilator from service, labeled unit Out of Service, documented TF 5513 event log findings, and referred device for qualified bench evaluation and repair.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 9708 Emergency buzzer self-test failure
description: Troubleshooting TF 9708 when the Hamilton G5 emergency buzzer fails self-test, creating risk that backup audible alarming may not function reliably even if ventilation continues.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the Hamilton G5 is connected to a patient, provide alternative ventilation or transfer the patient to another approved ventilator before troubleshooting. Do not rely on a ventilator with a potentially unavailable emergency audible alarm.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 9708 — Emergency buzzer self-test failure. Document whether it occurs during startup, after power-up, during ventilation, or repeatedly after restart, and note any additional alarm or audible-warning concerns.

steps.title: Remove the Ventilator From Active Clinical Use
steps.instructions: Once alternate ventilation is in place, remove the Hamilton G5 from patient use and attach an Out of Service label identifying TF 9708 and the unresolved audible alarm reliability concern.

steps.title: Check the Event Log
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 9708 in the event log and review for repeated occurrences, date and time of the fault, startup versus operational occurrence, and additional nearby alarm-system or technical fault entries.

steps.title: Check External and Simple Conditions
steps.instructions: Inspect the ventilator externally without disassembly. Confirm known-good AC power, secure undamaged power cord, normal power-up, and absence of visible damage, contamination, impact evidence, abnormal heat, odors, sounds, or associated power and alarm faults.

steps.title: Confirm the Fault During a Safe Non-Patient Check
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from patient use, complete normal startup or pre-use observation according to facility procedure. Determine whether TF 9708 returns or whether additional alarm-system concerns are indicated.

steps.title: Verify Repair and Alarm Function Before Return to Service
steps.instructions: Return the ventilator to clinical use only after qualified bench evaluation or repair and successful functional and alarm verification checks confirming proper emergency buzzer operation.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed TF 9708 — Emergency buzzer self-test failure. Ventilator continued ventilation, but emergency audible alarm reliability could not be confirmed.
CCR.Cause: Technical fault TF 9708 confirmed on display and/or in event log. No visible external damage, power cord issue, outlet issue, or other simple external cause identified. Emergency buzzer self-test failure requires further service evaluation.
CCR.Resolution: Confirmed alternative ventilation before troubleshooting. Removed ventilator from clinical service, labeled unit Out of Service, documented TF 9708 event log findings, and routed unit for qualified bench evaluation or repair before return to use.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 9416 High-pressure alarm limit value is incorrect in DPRAM
description: Troubleshooting TF 9416 when an invalid high-pressure alarm limit value in DPRAM causes a high-priority alarm and places the ventilator into ambient state.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Immediately provide alternative ventilation using an approved backup ventilator or manual ventilation method according to clinical protocol. Do not continue relying on the Hamilton G5 after TF 9416 occurs or while the ventilator is in ambient state.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm that the ventilator displays TF 9416, sounds a high-priority alarm, and indicates that it entered ambient state. Determine whether the error occurred during startup, active ventilation, setup changes, or intermittently during operation.

steps.title: Remove the Ventilator From Patient Use
steps.instructions: Once alternate ventilation is established, disconnect the Hamilton G5 from patient care and label the ventilator Out of Service so it cannot be returned to patient use accidentally.

steps.title: Check External Power and Physical Condition
steps.instructions: Confirm AC power and power cord security, determine whether battery operation or a power interruption occurred, and inspect externally for liquid intrusion, impact damage, loose external connections, unusual odor, abnormal heat, or contamination. Do not open the ventilator during initial troubleshooting.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: After the unit is removed from patient use, confirm the TF 9416 event log entry, document its date and time, determine whether it occurred once or repeatedly, and record any associated technical faults, restart events, or power events.

steps.title: Interpret the Error Correctly
steps.instructions: Recognize TF 9416 as an internal DPRAM high-pressure alarm limit value technical fault, not a routine high airway pressure alarm caused by a circuit obstruction, patient condition, or alarm limit adjustment.

steps.title: Escalate for Repair Evaluation
steps.instructions: Keep the ventilator out of service and contact Hamilton Medical technical support or follow the approved repair escalation process. Provide the device serial number, fault code, event log findings, ambient state behavior, and observed external conditions.

steps.title: Return to Service Only After Approved Resolution
steps.instructions: Return the ventilator to patient use only after approved corrective action has been completed and all required operational, alarm, and safety verification checks have passed.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed TF 9416 High-pressure alarm limit value is incorrect in DPRAM, sounded a high-priority alarm, and entered ambient state during reported operation.
CCR.Cause: Verified TF 9416 in the event log indicating an internal DPRAM high-pressure alarm limit value error. No external power, circuit, accessory, or visible physical condition identified that would correct the reported fault.
CCR.Resolution: Patient ventilation transferred to an approved alternate method by clinical staff. Ventilator removed from service, labeled Out of Service, event log findings documented, and unit referred for Hamilton Medical technical support or qualified repair evaluation.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 9417 Apnea Time Data Fault
description: Troubleshooting TF 9417 when incorrect apnea time data in DPRAM causes a high-priority alarm and forces the Hamilton G5 into ambient state, resulting in loss of active mechanical ventilation.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Treat TF 9417 as an immediate patient safety event. Provide alternative ventilation immediately using an approved backup ventilator or manual ventilation method directed by clinical staff. Do not troubleshoot while the Hamilton G5 is the patient's only means of ventilatory support.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: After alternative ventilation is established, confirm TF 9417, any high-priority audible alarm, and whether the ventilator entered ambient state or stopped normal ventilation operation. Document when the fault occurred.

steps.title: Remove the Affected Ventilator From Patient Use
steps.instructions: Disconnect the Hamilton G5 from patient use after backup ventilation is established. Do not return the device to service because the error clears after restart or appears intermittent.

steps.title: Inspect External Conditions
steps.instructions: Check the AC power connection, power cord condition, exterior condition, breathing circuit, and accessories for visible damage, contamination, heat, odor, or disconnection. Document whether the event followed transport, power interruption, accessory replacement, or configuration change.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: With the patient safely supported elsewhere, review the event log for TF 9417, date and time, repeated occurrences, related technical faults, and confirmation that the ventilator entered ambient state.

steps.title: Do Not Treat TF 9417 as a Correctable Bedside Setting Issue
steps.instructions: Do not assume that adjusting the apnea time setting corrects the fault. TF 9417 indicates incorrect internal apnea time data in DPRAM and requires repair evaluation before reuse.

steps.title: Remove the Ventilator From Service
steps.instructions: Label the unit Out of Service and send it for bench evaluation or manufacturer-authorized repair. Include fault behavior and event log findings with the service request. Return to use only after repair and required verification are completed.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed Error TF 9417, generated a high-priority alarm, and entered ambient state during operation, resulting in loss of active ventilator support.
CCR.Cause: TF 9417 confirmed in the event log. Fault indicates incorrect apnea time value in DPRAM. No external damage, circuit issue, or power connection problem found that would safely explain or resolve the condition.
CCR.Resolution: Patient ventilation transferred to an alternate approved method by clinical staff. Ventilator removed from service and labeled Out of Service. Event log reviewed and fault documented. Unit sent for bench evaluation or manufacturer-authorized repair before return to clinical use.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 8000 Alarm Queue Could Not Be Opened
description: Troubleshooting TF 8000 when the ventilator cannot provide alarm messages and enters ambient state, making it unsafe for clinical ventilation use.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the Hamilton G5 is connected to a patient or prepared for immediate clinical use, provide alternative ventilation immediately using an approved backup ventilator or manual ventilation method as directed by clinical staff. Do not continue relying on the ventilator because it has entered ambient state and cannot provide alarm messages.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm technical fault TF 8000, high-priority alarm behavior, entry into ambient state, and loss of normal alarm message capability. Determine whether the fault occurred during startup, active ventilation, after a power cycle, or intermittently.

steps.title: Remove the Ventilator From Clinical Use
steps.instructions: Once alternative ventilation is established, disconnect the Hamilton G5 from patient use, label it Out of Service, and do not return it to service based only on a restart or temporary clearing of the fault.

steps.title: Perform Basic External Safety Checks
steps.instructions: With the device off the patient, confirm the AC power connection is secure, inspect the power cord and plug for damage, inspect for impact damage, fluid intrusion, contamination, overheating, or unusual odor, and document whether the error followed a move, drop, cleaning incident, or power interruption.

steps.title: Confirm the Fault Is Not an Accessory or Setup Issue
steps.instructions: Document connected accessories present when the fault occurred, but do not spend extended time troubleshooting circuits, sensors, gas hoses, humidifiers, settings, or optional accessories as the primary cause of TF 8000. Do not return the ventilator to use based on accessory replacement.

steps.title: Record Available Fault Information
steps.instructions: Document TF 8000, the time and circumstances of occurrence, whether ambient state was confirmed, whether a high-priority alarm sounded, whether the fault occurred during startup or active ventilation, and any accessible event log findings.

steps.title: Escalate for Manufacturer Support or Bench Evaluation
steps.instructions: Contact Hamilton Medical technical support or follow the facility's authorized repair pathway. Do not attempt unauthorized internal repair or return the ventilator to service until approved evaluation confirms proper ventilation and alarm operation.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed Error TF 8000, sounded a high-priority alarm, and entered ambient state. Reported condition indicates alarm messages could not be provided.
CCR.Cause: Technical fault TF 8000 indicates failure of the ventilator alarm queue function. External inspection did not identify a correctable power, accessory, or visible damage issue. Device cannot be considered safe for ventilation use without repair evaluation.
CCR.Resolution: Alternative ventilation was provided before troubleshooting. Hamilton G5 was removed from service, labeled Out of Service, fault details documented, and unit referred for Hamilton Medical technical support or authorized bench evaluation.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 8803 Communication interface option not found
description: Troubleshooting TF 8803 when the Hamilton G5 cannot detect or communicate through its external communication interface while ventilation continues.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Confirm the patient is receiving appropriate ventilation and that no additional ventilator alarms or changes in therapy are present. If external communication is clinically required, provide a backup ventilator or approved alternate communication method before troubleshooting.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 8803 and the message Communications interface option not found. Determine whether the condition occurs at startup, after connecting an external device, after configuration changes, or intermittently during use.

steps.title: Inspect External Communication Connections
steps.instructions: Inspect externally accessible communication cables and connectors for loose connections, damaged pins, damaged cable insulation, contamination, or an incorrect cable. Reseat or replace an approved external cable when appropriate.

steps.title: Verify the Connected Device and Protocol Compatibility
steps.instructions: Confirm that the connected external device and interface setup are intended for the Hamilton G5 and use the appropriate supported communication method, such as Hamilton Medical protocol or VueLink protocol.

steps.title: Determine Whether the Communication Interface Is Clinically Required
steps.instructions: Confirm whether staff require interface communication for monitoring or documentation. If communication is not clinically required, qualified personnel may disable the interface according to approved procedures and facility policy.

steps.title: Check Whether the Error Clears After External Corrections
steps.instructions: After confirming cable condition, connection, compatible device, protocol, and configuration, observe whether TF 8803 returns. Document the correction if normal communication is restored.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: Review the event log through the approved service process for repeated TF 8803 occurrences, related communication faults, timing patterns, or signs of an intermittent condition.

steps.title: Escalate for Qualified Bench Evaluation
steps.instructions: If the fault persists after external causes are ruled out, remove the ventilator from communication-dependent service and send it for qualified bench evaluation of the VIP software or EPROM and interface hardware, including the Interface Board when indicated.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed TF 8803 - Communications interface option not found. Ventilation continued, but external communication interface data was unavailable.
CCR.Cause: Confirmed TF 8803 technical fault. Inspected external communication cable and verified connected device/protocol setup. Fault persisted after external checks, indicating possible VIP software/EPROM or Interface Board-related failure.
CCR.Resolution: Confirmed alternate communication plan with clinical staff, reviewed event log, labeled ventilator Out of Service, and sent unit for bench evaluation of the communication interface system.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 8802 Communication interface failure
description: Troubleshooting TF 8802 when the ventilator cannot establish communication with an external interface after repeated attempts while ventilation may continue.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the ventilator is connected to a patient, coordinate with clinical staff and provide alternative ventilation before removing the unit from service or performing extended troubleshooting. Do not rely on continued ventilation as proof that the device is fully safe for continued clinical use.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 8802 is displayed, determine when the fault occurs, verify whether ventilation continues, and review the event log for repeated or related communication faults.

steps.title: Identify the Connected Communication Device
steps.instructions: Determine what external communication device or interface system is connected. Confirm the intended connection is being used and inspect accessible connections for looseness, damage, contamination, or bent pins.

steps.title: Check the Communication Cable and External Connections
steps.instructions: Inspect the communication cable and connectors for damage, strain, contamination, bent pins, incorrect adapters, or loose connections. Substitute an approved known-good cable when available.

steps.title: Confirm External Device Protocol Availability
steps.instructions: Confirm the connected device or interface system is configured and able to open the required VueLink protocol. Coordinate with monitoring, integration, or IT support when appropriate.

steps.title: Isolate Whether the Fault Follows the Ventilator or External Setup
steps.instructions: When clinically safe, use a known-good compatible communication setup or ventilator to determine whether the failure follows the cable, external system, interface configuration, or ventilator.

steps.title: Check Software or Interface Version Requirements
steps.instructions: If external checks do not resolve the fault, confirm through qualified service support whether the VIP EPROM is at the latest applicable version. Do not perform internal modifications during clinical use.

steps.title: Stop When Resolved and Verify Operation
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 8802 no longer appears, verify normal communication, review the event log for recurrence, complete required operational checks, and document corrective action before returning the ventilator to service.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed Error TF 8802 during communication interface startup. Unit attempted communication repeatedly without establishing connection; ventilation continued while technical fault remained displayed.
CCR.Cause: Inspected external communication setup and verified cable connections. Fault persisted after accessible external causes were ruled out, indicating likely ventilator communication interface failure or service-level VueLink/VIP EPROM compatibility issue.
CCR.Resolution: Removed ventilator from clinical service, labeled unit Out of Service, reviewed event log for TF 8802 occurrences, and forwarded unit for bench evaluation of interface version compatibility and Interface Board condition.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 8607 Icon File or British English Language String File Not Found
description: Troubleshooting TF 8607 when required display words or icons are missing, creating an unsafe ventilator user-interface condition even if ventilation appears to continue.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot while the ventilator is supporting a patient with an incomplete display. Notify clinical staff and move the patient to a working backup ventilator before continuing.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Display Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm TF 8607 is displayed and document whether words, icons, or other interface elements are missing, including when the fault occurs.

steps.title: Check External Power and Startup Stability
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to known-good AC power and observe for stable operation, additional technical faults, unexpected shutdowns, or restarts.

steps.title: Inspect the Display and External Physical Condition
steps.instructions: Inspect the screen, bezel, and housing for visible damage, contamination, fluid intrusion, or abnormal display behavior without opening the ventilator.

steps.title: Confirm the Interface and Language Symptoms
steps.instructions: Determine whether missing words or icons match the reported display-resource failure and do not return the device to patient use solely because ventilation appears to continue.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: With the device removed from clinical use, review and document TF 8607 and any associated startup, software, media, or display-related technical faults.

steps.title: Determine Whether the Device Can Be Released
steps.instructions: Release the ventilator only if the complete interface returns, no technical faults remain, alarms and controls are readable, and required operational verification is completed.

steps.title: Escalate Persistent TF 8607
steps.instructions: If the fault persists after external checks, remove the ventilator from service, label it Out of Service, and send it for authorized bench repair involving SW Program CompactFlash replacement and post-repair verification.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed TF 8607. Screen was missing required words and/or icons while the unit appeared to continue functioning.
CCR.Cause: Confirmed persistent TF 8607 with incomplete display interface. External power was stable and no obvious external display damage was observed. Fault indicates required icon or British English language-string file could not be found.
CCR.Resolution: Removed ventilator from service, labeled unit Out of Service, reviewed event log, and escalated for authorized bench repair involving SW Program CompactFlash replacement and post-repair verification.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 9612 Invalid air pressure detected outside the range of 500 to 1000 mbar
description: Troubleshooting Error TF 9612 when the Hamilton G5 detects an invalid ambient air-pressure value, activates a high-priority alarm, and substitutes a default pressure value of 760 mmHg.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the Hamilton G5 is actively ventilating a patient and displays TF 9612, notify clinical staff immediately. Transfer the patient to another approved ventilator or backup ventilation method before troubleshooting the device.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm the displayed technical fault is TF 9612. Document whether it occurred during startup, pre-use checks, active ventilation, intermittently, or after movement between locations or elevations. Confirm high-priority alarm behavior, event-log recording, and use of the default air-pressure value of 760 mmHg.

steps.title: Remove the Ventilator From Patient Use for Evaluation
steps.instructions: Once alternate ventilation is established, remove the Hamilton G5 from clinical use for evaluation. Label the ventilator according to department procedure if the technical fault remains active or occurred during patient ventilation.

steps.title: Check the Ventilator Environment and Physical Condition
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator is in a normal hospital environment. Check for recent elevation change, extreme temperature or humidity, liquid intrusion, heavy contamination, impact, tipping, physical damage, blocked openings, or fluid exposure.

steps.title: Verify Basic Power and Startup Conditions
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to a known-good AC power source and confirm normal power indicators. Power on the ventilator according to normal Clinical Engineering evaluation practice and observe whether TF 9612 reappears during startup or pre-use checks.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: Access the event log and confirm TF 9612. Document the date and time, whether the fault occurred once or repeatedly, other technical faults near the same time, and whether the event correlates with startup, movement, loss of power, or active operation.

steps.title: Determine Whether the Error Has Cleared or Persists
steps.instructions: Observe whether the ventilator completes required pre-use checks without TF 9612 returning. If the fault returns, remains active, or is repeated in the event log, do not return the ventilator to patient use; remove it from service for repair or bench evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator reported Error TF 9612: Invalid air pressure detected outside the range of 500 to 1000 mbar. High-priority alarm activated and ventilator substituted the default air-pressure value of 760 mmHg.
CCR.Cause: Event log confirmed TF 9612. External inspection, normal hospital environmental conditions, and known-good AC power did not identify an external cause. Technical fault reoccurred during controlled startup/pre-use evaluation, indicating likely internal air-pressure detection fault.
CCR.Resolution: Removed Hamilton G5 from service, labeled unit Out of Service, documented event-log findings, and referred ventilator for bench evaluation or manufacturer-authorized repair due to persistent TF 9612.

title: Hamilton G5 Ventilator - Error: TF 9704 A/D converter offset or status is out of specification at VUP startup
description: Troubleshooting TF 9704 when an A/D converter startup fault causes the Hamilton G5 ventilator to alarm and enter ambient state, preventing dependable ventilation.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Immediately provide alternative ventilation using an approved backup ventilator or manual ventilation method according to clinical protocol. Do not rely on the Hamilton G5 while TF 9704 is displayed or while the ventilator is in ambient state.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm the exact displayed technical fault is TF 9704. Document whether the fault occurs during startup or after restart and whether the ventilator sounds a high-priority alarm, enters ambient state, or fails to provide normal ventilation.

steps.title: Remove the Ventilator From Clinical Use
steps.instructions: After alternate ventilation is established, disconnect the ventilator from patient use and apply an Out of Service label identifying TF 9704 and ambient state entry.

steps.title: Check External Power and Physical Condition
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to a known-good AC power source for evaluation. Inspect for visible damage, fluid intrusion, contamination, overheating, unusual odor, damaged power cord, or loose external connections.

steps.title: Review the Event Log
steps.instructions: Access the event log according to approved service procedures. Confirm the recorded TF 9704 event and document the date, time, recurrence, related faults, and whether the fault occurs at startup.

steps.title: Perform the A/D Converter Check in Test Mode
steps.instructions: With the ventilator removed from patient use, perform the A/D Converter Check in Test Mode using the approved Hamilton service procedure. Record whether the test passes or confirms an out-of-specification condition.

steps.title: Complete Return-to-Service Verification Only if the Fault Is Cleared
steps.instructions: Return the ventilator to service only after TF 9704 is absent and all required functional verification has been completed. If the error recurs, the A/D Converter Check fails, or ambient state continues, remove the device from service and escalate for repair.

CCR.Complaint: Hamilton G5 ventilator displayed TF 9704 during startup, sounded a high-priority alarm, and entered ambient state, preventing normal ventilation.
CCR.Cause: Confirmed TF 9704 indicating A/D converter offset or status out of specification at VUP startup. External inspection and known-good AC power check found no obvious contributing issue. Event log was reviewed and A/D Converter Check was performed in Test Mode.
CCR.Resolution: Alternative ventilation was provided before troubleshooting. Ventilator was removed from service, labeled Out of Service — TF 9704 / Ambient State, event log findings were documented, and unit was routed for qualified bench repair or Hamilton technical support evaluation.

title: Hamilton C6 Ventilator - Preoperational Check or Circuit Test Failure
description: Troubleshooting failed tightness tests or preoperational checks caused by circuit leaks, incorrect connections, flow sensors, humidifiers, or expiratory valve installation.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a failed preoperational check while the HAMILTON-C6 is supporting a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Confirm that the replacement device passes its required checks and provides effective ventilation. Place the affected HAMILTON-C6 in Standby before changing circuit components. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on a ventilator that has not passed its preoperational check. Hamilton specifies that the preoperational check should be completed after installing a new breathing circuit or flow sensor and before connecting the patient.

steps.title: 2. Identify Which Test Failed
steps.instructions: Open System > Tests & calib, or select Preop check from the Standby window. Determine whether the failure involves: Tightness test; Flow sensor calibration; O₂ sensor calibration; CO₂ sensor calibration; Startup self-test or alarm function. Record the red X, displayed message, and completion time. Expected outcome: The failed portion of the preoperational check is clearly identified so troubleshooting can remain focused.

steps.title: 3. Confirm the Correct Test Setup
steps.instructions: Verify that the ventilator is configured with the complete circuit intended for use, including: Inspiratory and expiratory limbs; Flow sensor; Expiratory valve set; Filters; Water traps; Humidifier and chamber, when used; CO₂ airway adapter, when used. Check that the selected patient group and circuit components are compatible. Expected outcome: The ventilator is being tested with a complete, correctly configured breathing system. If anything was missing or incorrectly installed, correct the setup and repeat the failed test. Stop if the check passes.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Breathing Circuit for Leaks or Disconnections
steps.instructions: Trace the circuit from the ventilator to the patient connection. Check for: Loose inspiratory or expiratory connections; Partially seated hoses; Cracked tubing or connectors; Open suction, nebulizer, sampling, or monitoring ports; Loose water-trap caps; Damaged filter housings; Poorly seated humidifier chamber; Unused ports without caps; Incorrectly assembled coaxial circuit components. Push each connection fully into place without forcing it. Expected outcome: The circuit is continuous, correctly assembled, and free of visible leakage points. Repeat the tightness test. If it passes, document the loose or leaking connection and stop. Hamilton lists circuit disconnection, incorrect connection, and leakage as the first items to check after a failed preoperational test.

steps.title: 5. Perform the Tightness Test Correctly
steps.instructions: Start the tightness test and follow the screen prompts exactly. When instructed: Disconnect the circuit at the patient side of the flow sensor; Block the flow-sensor opening completely; Maintain a firm seal until the ventilator indicates that the test is finished. Wear a clean glove and follow facility infection-control procedures when occluding the opening. Expected outcome: The ventilator displays a green check and records the test completion date and time. An incomplete seal, blocking the wrong location, or releasing the opening too early can produce an apparent failure.

steps.title: 6. Inspect the Flow Sensor and Tubing
steps.instructions: Verify that: The correct Hamilton-compatible flow sensor is installed; The sensor is fully connected at the Y-piece or designated circuit position; Both flow-sensor tubing connections are secure; Tubing is not crossed, kinked, pinched, cracked, or disconnected; The sensor is dry and free of contamination; The sensor body is not visibly cracked or deformed. Reconnect the sensor and tubing securely. Expected outcome: The flow sensor and its pressure lines are correctly installed and intact. Repeat the failed check. If it passes, stop. Hamilton identifies the flow sensor as the next component to inspect after the breathing circuit.

steps.title: 7. Repeat the Flow Sensor Calibration
steps.instructions: Select Flow sensor under Tests & calib. Follow each prompt: Attach the calibration adapter; Rotate the sensor and adapter 180 degrees as instructed; Wait for the ventilator to complete that portion of the calibration; Rotate the sensor back; Remove the calibration adapter when prompted. Do not skip a prompt or rotate the sensor before instructed. Expected outcome: A green check and updated completion time appear. If calibration passes, reinstall the sensor in its normal operating position and stop.

steps.title: 8. Inspect and Reseat the Expiratory Valve Set
steps.instructions: Remove the expiratory valve set only while the ventilator is out of patient use. Check that: The silicone membrane is present; The membrane lies flat without folds, tears, warping, or contamination; The membrane’s metal plate faces upward and remains visible; The valve housing is clean and undamaged; The assembly is fully inserted and rotated clockwise into the locked position. Reinstall the valve set carefully. Expected outcome: The expiratory valve assembly is properly installed and seated. Repeat the failed test. If the check passes, stop. Hamilton’s setup instructions specify correct membrane orientation and secure locking of the expiratory valve housing.

steps.title: 9. Isolate the Humidifier
steps.instructions: When a humidifier is installed, temporarily configure the test circuit without it, using an approved setup. Repeat the tightness test. If the test passes without the humidifier: Inspect the chamber, seals, adapters, temperature-probe ports, and circuit connections for leakage. If the test still fails: Continue troubleshooting the circuit, flow sensor, and expiratory valve. Expected outcome: The humidifier is either identified or ruled out as the leakage source. Hamilton specifically recommends repeating a failed preoperational test without the humidifier and checking the humidifier setup for leaks if the test then succeeds.

steps.title: 10. Substitute Known-Good External Components
steps.instructions: Replace one component at a time with a compatible known-good item: Breathing circuit; Flow sensor; Expiratory valve set; Humidifier chamber or associated adapter, when implicated. Repeat the failed test after each substitution. Avoid replacing several components simultaneously unless immediate isolation is not required. Expected outcome: The defective external component is identified and the preoperational check passes. Hamilton’s documented troubleshooting sequence recommends replacing the breathing circuit, flow sensor, and expiratory valve set before referring the ventilator for service.

steps.title: 11. Complete the Remaining Required Checks
steps.instructions: Once the tightness test and flow-sensor calibration pass: Perform O₂ sensor calibration when indicated; Perform CO₂ sensor calibration when installed and required; Verify that the startup self-test produced the expected audible alarm; Confirm that all required tests display a green check; Perform a functional verification using an appropriate test lung before returning the device to service. Expected outcome: The ventilator passes its preoperational checks and operates normally with the intended circuit configuration. Do not return the ventilator to clinical use with an unresolved failed check. The C6 quick guide states that the ventilator should only be used after it passes all tests.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the HAMILTON-C6 failed the preoperational tightness test and displayed a red failure indicator.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found the expiratory valve membrane folded under the valve housing, preventing the valve set from sealing correctly.
CCR.Resolution: Reinstalled the membrane with the metal plate facing upward, secured the expiratory valve set, and completed the tightness test, flow-sensor calibration, and test-lung verification successfully.

helpfulDetails: Exact failed test or displayed message
Test results before and after repair
Unusual sounds, heat, odor, or leakage

title: Hamilton C6 Ventilator - Flow Sensor Calibration Failure
description: Troubleshooting failed flow-sensor calibration caused by incorrect sensor selection, loose tubing, circuit leaks, moisture, improper seating, or defective external components.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not perform flow-sensor calibration while the ventilator is connected to a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Provide manual ventilation when clinically required and performed by qualified personnel. Confirm adequate ventilation and monitoring before continuing. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on inaccurate flow, volume, or pressure measurements. The C6 identifies missing or unusable flow-sensor calibration data as a high-priority condition.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Reported Failure
steps.instructions: Place the ventilator in Standby and open: System > Tests & calib > Flow sensor. Determine whether: Calibration will not begin. The display repeatedly requests that the sensor be turned. Calibration completes with a red X. A “Flow sensor calibration needed” alarm remains active. The problem began after changing the circuit, flow sensor, humidifier, or expiratory valve. Record the exact displayed message and whether the failure occurs every time. Expected outcome: The failure condition is clearly identified before components are changed.

steps.title: 3. Verify the Selected Patient Group
steps.instructions: Confirm that the installed flow sensor matches the selected patient group: Adult/pediatric flow sensor for the Adult/Ped patient group. Neonatal/pediatric flow sensor when configured for neonatal use. A mismatch between the selected patient group and installed flow sensor will cause calibration to fail. Expected outcome: The correct sensor type and patient category are selected. If correcting the patient group resolves calibration, complete the remaining preoperational checks and stop.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Flow Sensor
steps.instructions: Remove the sensor from clinical use and inspect it externally for: Cracks or deformation. Damaged connection nipples. Contamination. Condensate or medication residue. A visibly damaged internal membrane. Incorrect or incompatible sensor type. Do not insert tools or compressed air into the sensor. When active humidification is used, accumulated water can interfere with proximal flow measurement. Hamilton recommends positioning the flow sensor at least 45 degrees relative to the floor to reduce water accumulation. Expected outcome: The sensor is clean, dry, undamaged, and appropriate for the circuit.

steps.title: 5. Check the Flow-Sensor Tubing and Connections
steps.instructions: Inspect both flow-sensor pressure tubes from the sensor to the ventilator. Confirm that: Both tubes are fully attached. The tubes are connected to their corresponding flow-sensor ports. No tube is kinked, pinched, stretched, cracked, wet, or obstructed. The connector fittings are not loose or damaged. No accessories are pulling on the tubing. Reseat each connection firmly without forcing it. Expected outcome: Both differential-pressure pathways are open and securely connected. If reseating the tubing resolves calibration, complete the preoperational check and stop.

steps.title: 6. Inspect the Breathing Circuit for Large Leaks
steps.instructions: Check the complete test circuit between the ventilator and flow sensor, including: Inspiratory and expiratory limbs. Y-piece. Humidifier chamber and connections. Water traps. Filters and adapters. Test lung connection. Unused ports or open sampling connections. Reconnect any loose component and replace visibly damaged tubing or accessories. Hamilton identifies circuit disconnections and large leaks, including leaks around the humidifier, as causes of failed flow-sensor calibration. Expected outcome: The circuit is complete, correctly assembled, and free of obvious leaks.

steps.title: 7. Check the Expiratory Valve Set
steps.instructions: Remove and reinstall the expiratory valve set according to the approved user-level setup procedure. Confirm that: The valve set is fully seated. The membrane is correctly positioned. The membrane is not folded, torn, hardened, wet, or visibly contaminated. The valve housing is not cracked or obstructed. The assembly locks into place normally. Improper seating of the flow sensor, expiratory valve set, or valve membrane can prevent successful calibration. Expected outcome: The expiratory valve and membrane are properly assembled and seated.

steps.title: 8. Repeat the Calibration Correctly
steps.instructions: With the patient disconnected: Assemble the complete breathing circuit and flow sensor. Select System > Tests & calib. Touch Flow sensor. Follow each screen prompt. Install the calibration adapter when instructed. Turn the flow sensor only when prompted. Return it to its starting orientation when prompted. Remove the adapter when instructed. Verify that a checkmark appears in the Flow Sensor checkbox. A red X indicates unsuccessful calibration. Expected outcome: Calibration completes with a checkmark. If calibration passes, perform the tightness test and remaining required preoperational checks before returning the ventilator to service.

steps.title: 9. Substitute a Known-Good Flow Sensor
steps.instructions: Install a compatible, known-good Hamilton flow sensor and repeat the calibration. Use the correct calibration adapter when required. Expected outcome: If calibration passes, the original flow sensor is defective or unsuitable. If calibration still fails, continue troubleshooting the valve and circuit. Do not return the original sensor to use unless it passes inspection and calibration.

steps.title: 10. Substitute External Circuit Components
steps.instructions: If the known-good sensor also fails, replace external components one at a time and repeat calibration after each change: Expiratory valve membrane. Complete expiratory valve set. Breathing circuit. Humidifier chamber or associated circuit section, when installed. Hamilton’s specified sequence after persistent failure is to replace the flow sensor, expiratory valve membrane, and expiratory valve before requesting service. Expected outcome: The defective external component is isolated.

steps.title: 11. Perform the Tightness Test and Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After successful calibration: Run the breathing-circuit tightness test. Confirm that the test passes. Connect an appropriate test lung. Verify stable pressure, flow, and volume readings. Confirm that monitored tidal volume responds normally. Check for unexpected alarms. Complete the required preoperational check. The C6 requires flow-sensor calibration and a circuit tightness test after installing a new or reprocessed circuit component. Expected outcome: The ventilator passes calibration, tightness testing, and functional verification without alarms.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Hamilton C6 displayed a red X during flow-sensor calibration and would not complete the preoperational check.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found condensate inside the adult/pediatric flow sensor and moisture within one flow-sensor pressure tube.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced the flow sensor and affected tubing, successfully completed flow-sensor calibration and circuit tightness testing, verified operation with a test lung, and returned the ventilator to service.

helpfulDetails: Patient group and sensor type verified
Calibration red X or checkmark observed
Expiratory valve membrane or valve replaced

title: Hamilton C6 Ventilator - O₂ Sensor Calibration Failure or Incorrect FiO₂
description: Troubleshooting failed O₂ sensor calibration or inaccurate displayed FiO₂ caused by gas supply, connections, calibration conditions, settings, or sensor failure.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot unreliable oxygen delivery or measurement while the HAMILTON-C6 is actively supporting a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Use independent oxygen monitoring when clinically required. Confirm that the replacement ventilator is delivering the prescribed oxygen concentration. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on uncertain FiO₂ delivery or monitoring. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the ventilator has been removed from patient use.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Failure
steps.instructions: Review the displayed alarm, message, and alarm history. Determine whether: O₂ sensor calibration will not begin. Calibration starts but fails. An O₂ sensor calibration needed alarm is displayed. Measured oxygen differs from the set FiO₂. The reading is unstable, delayed, or fixed at one value. The issue occurs only at higher oxygen settings. The problem began after a gas-supply, sensor, or configuration change. Record the set FiO₂, displayed oxygen value, gas-source status, and exact message. Expected outcome: The failure pattern is clearly identified before components are changed.

steps.title: 3. Verify the Oxygen Supply
steps.instructions: Confirm that the oxygen hose is: Connected to the correct ventilator inlet. Fully seated at both the ventilator and wall or cylinder source. Free of kinks, crushing, damage, and obvious leakage. Not crossed with the compressed-air hose. Verify the oxygen source has adequate pressure and is not empty, shut off, or intermittently failing. When permitted, test the outlet using an approved gas-pressure analyzer or a known-good device. An inadequate oxygen source can cause both calibration failure and incorrect delivered FiO₂. Expected outcome: A stable oxygen supply is available at the ventilator inlet. If correcting the gas supply resolves the issue, repeat the required preoperational checks and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 4. Check the Air Supply
steps.instructions: Verify that the compressed-air connection is also correct and stable. Incorrect air pressure, a crossed hose, or loss of one gas source can affect the ventilator’s oxygen blending and make the displayed or measured FiO₂ appear incorrect. Expected outcome: Both required gas sources are correctly connected and available.

steps.title: 5. Inspect External Gas Connections
steps.instructions: Inspect the oxygen and air fittings for: Loose connections. Damaged threads or couplings. Contamination. Bent or damaged fittings. Audible leakage. Incorrect adapters. Excessive tension on the hoses. Substitute known-good, compatible gas hoses when available. Expected outcome: The ventilator receives gas through secure, undamaged connections. If replacing a defective hose or fitting restores normal operation, complete operational verification and stop.

steps.title: 6. Verify the Oxygen Setting and Alarm Limits
steps.instructions: Confirm that the selected oxygen concentration matches the intended test value. Review: Set Oxygen or FiO₂ value. Oxygen alarm limits. Active ventilation mode. Any automated oxygen-control features. Patient-category and configuration settings. Ensure the complaint is not caused by comparing the measured oxygen value with an outdated prescription, previous patient setup, or automatically adjusted setting. Expected outcome: The intended oxygen setting and alarm configuration are confirmed.

steps.title: 7. Allow Adequate Stabilization Time
steps.instructions: After connecting gas supplies or changing the oxygen setting, operate the ventilator on an approved test lung and allow the oxygen concentration to stabilize. A brief difference between the set and displayed value may occur immediately after startup or a major FiO₂ adjustment. Persistent or excessive deviation requires further evaluation. Expected outcome: The displayed oxygen value stabilizes near the selected setting.

steps.title: 8. Prepare the Ventilator for O₂ Sensor Calibration
steps.instructions: Place the ventilator in the condition required by its installed software and sensor configuration. Follow the on-screen calibration instructions exactly. Before starting: Confirm both gas supplies are stable. Confirm there are no active gas-supply alarms. Use the correct patient circuit and test lung. Ensure the circuit is assembled without major leaks. Confirm the ventilator is not connected to a patient. Allow the O₂ sensor sufficient warm-up time when applicable. The HAMILTON-C6 includes an O₂ sensor calibration function and can generate an O₂ sensor calibration needed alarm when calibration is required. Expected outcome: The ventilator is in a stable and appropriate condition for calibration.

steps.title: 9. Run the O₂ Sensor Calibration
steps.instructions: Initiate the O₂ sensor calibration from the appropriate System, Tests & Calib, or preoperational-check screen for the installed software version. Follow all displayed prompts without disconnecting gas supplies or changing settings during calibration. Expected outcome: Calibration completes successfully and the calibration-needed message clears. If calibration succeeds, continue to independent FiO₂ verification before returning the ventilator to service.

steps.title: 10. Repeat Calibration After Correcting External Conditions
steps.instructions: If calibration fails: Reconfirm oxygen and air source pressures. Reseat both gas hoses. Check for active supply alarms. Allow additional sensor stabilization time. Restart the calibration once. Do not repeatedly calibrate a sensor without correcting the condition causing the failure. Expected outcome: A temporary connection, pressure, or stabilization issue is corrected.

steps.title: 11. Inspect the Accessible O₂ Sensor Area
steps.instructions: With the ventilator powered down and removed from service, inspect only externally accessible sensor-related areas permitted by facility procedure. Look for: A loose or improperly seated accessible sensor. Contamination or moisture. Damaged accessible contacts. Signs of corrosion. Incorrect sensor type. Evidence that the sensor was recently replaced or disturbed. Do not perform deep internal disassembly or board-level troubleshooting. Expected outcome: No external sensor seating or contamination problem remains.

steps.title: 12. Compare Delivered FiO₂ With an Independent Analyzer
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to a suitable test lung and calibrated oxygen analyzer. Test several clinically relevant oxygen settings, such as: Approximately 21%. An intermediate concentration. A high oxygen concentration. Allow the reading to stabilize at each setting. Compare the independent analyzer reading with the set and displayed FiO₂. Use the manufacturer’s applicable specifications and facility test procedure to determine acceptance. Expected outcome: Delivered oxygen tracks the selected concentration within the permitted tolerance. If the external analyzer agrees with the set value but the ventilator display does not, suspect an O₂ sensing or calibration problem. If both the external analyzer and ventilator indicate incorrect oxygen delivery, suspect a gas-source, mixer, valve, or internal pneumatic problem.

steps.title: 13. Test With a Known-Good Approved O₂ Sensor When Authorized
steps.instructions: When the installed sensor is a replaceable item and facility policy permits, substitute a known-good Hamilton-approved compatible O₂ sensor. Repeat: O₂ sensor calibration. Preoperational checks. Independent FiO₂ testing. Do not install an unapproved or incompatible sensor. Expected outcome: Calibration and FiO₂ accuracy return to normal with the known-good sensor. If replacement resolves the issue, document the failed sensor and complete all required functional testing before return to service.

steps.title: 14. Perform the Complete Preoperational Check
steps.instructions: After any adjustment, hose substitution, calibration, or sensor replacement, perform the complete manufacturer-required preoperational check. Verify: Gas supplies. Circuit tightness. Flow-sensor function. O₂ sensor calibration. Alarm operation. Delivered oxygen concentration. Stable ventilation on a test lung. Expected outcome: All required tests pass without alarms or abnormal oxygen readings. If any required check fails, do not return the ventilator to clinical use.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the HAMILTON-C6 failed O₂ sensor calibration and displayed an FiO₂ value lower than the selected oxygen setting.
CCR.Cause: Verified stable wall air and oxygen supplies, then found that the installed O₂ sensor continued to fail calibration and produced unstable readings during independent oxygen testing.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the ventilator from service, replaced the approved O₂ sensor, successfully completed calibration and preoperational testing, and verified delivered FiO₂ with a calibrated oxygen analyzer.

title: Hamilton C6 Ventilator - High Pressure Alarm
description: Troubleshooting high-pressure alarms caused by circuit obstruction, flow-sensor tubing, expiratory components, accessories, alarm settings, or an internal ventilator fault.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions:
Do not troubleshoot a persistent high-pressure alarm while the HAMILTON-C6 is actively supporting a patient.

Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method before continuing. Provide manual ventilation when clinically necessary and performed by qualified personnel.

Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on a ventilator that may be limiting or interrupting delivered breaths.

Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the affected ventilator has been removed from patient use.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Alarm
steps.instructions:
Review the active alarm and alarm buffer. Determine whether the displayed message is:

High pressure
High pressure during sigh
High PEEP
Another pressure-related or expiratory-system alarm

Record the measured peak pressure, selected mode, PEEP, pressure settings, alarm limit, and whether the alarm occurs continuously or only during specific breaths.

On the HAMILTON-C6, the High pressure alarm occurs when measured inspiratory pressure exceeds the configured high Pressure alarm limit. The ventilator then stops inspiratory flow and opens the expiratory valve to reduce pressure.

Expected outcome: The exact alarm condition and circumstances are documented before equipment is changed.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Patient Circuit for Kinks or Compression
steps.instructions:
Examine the entire breathing circuit from the ventilator ports to the test lung or patient connection.

Check for:

Tubing trapped under equipment
Sharp bends or collapsed circuit limbs
Circuit tubing twisted around the support arm
Occluded connectors or adapters
Water accumulation blocking gas flow
A test lung or connection that is physically compressed

Correct any visible restriction and retest.

Expected outcome: The circuit remains fully open throughout inspiration and expiration.

If the alarm clears and pressure remains stable during testing, the obstruction was the likely cause. Stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Artificial-Airway Connection or Test Setup
steps.instructions:
When testing off the patient, inspect the test lung, airway adapter, elbow, catheter mount, and all connecting fittings.

Verify that:

The test lung is not stuck, damaged, or excessively restrictive.
The airway adapter is unobstructed.
No protective cap, packaging component, or plug remains installed.
The test setup is appropriate for the selected patient group and settings.

Hamilton specifically identifies artificial-airway kinks or occlusions as possible causes of a High pressure alarm.

Expected outcome: Gas can move freely through the complete test setup.

If replacing the test lung or adapter resolves the alarm, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 5. Check the Flow Sensor and Flow-Sensor Tubes
steps.instructions:
Inspect the flow sensor for contamination, incorrect installation, retained moisture, physical damage, or reversed orientation.

Check both flow-sensor tubes for:

Kinks
Pinching
Condensation
Loose connections
Incorrect port connection
Cracks or damage

Reseat the connections. Replace the flow sensor and tubing with known-good compatible components when available, then perform the required calibration or preoperational check.

Hamilton includes obstructed breathing-circuit limbs and flow-sensor tubes among the corrective checks for high-pressure conditions.

Expected outcome: The flow sensor is correctly installed, unobstructed, calibrated, and producing stable measurements.

If a known-good sensor assembly resolves the alarm, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 6. Inspect Filters, Humidifier, and Inline Accessories
steps.instructions:
Check every component placed in the gas pathway, including:

Inspiratory and expiratory filters
Heat-and-moisture exchanger
Humidifier chamber
Water traps
Nebulizer adapters
CO₂ airway adapters
Closed-suction components
Specialty connectors

Look for saturation, contamination, incorrect assembly, retained water, or excessive resistance. Temporarily replace questionable components with known-good compatible accessories.

Do not operate the ventilator clinically with required filters or safety components removed.

Expected outcome: All inline components are correctly installed and allow unrestricted gas flow.

If replacing an obstructed filter or accessory resolves the alarm, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 7. Inspect the Expiratory Limb and Expiratory Valve Set
steps.instructions:
Check the expiratory limb for kinks, water accumulation, contamination, and blocked fittings.

Remove and visually inspect the user-removable expiratory valve set according to facility procedures. Verify that it is:

Correctly assembled
Fully seated
Free of visible contamination
Not physically damaged
Appropriate for the selected circuit and patient group

Install a known-good compatible expiratory valve set when available.

Expected outcome: Exhaled gas passes through the expiratory pathway without abnormal resistance.

If the alarm clears with a known-good expiratory valve set, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 8. Verify the Circuit Configuration and Patient Group
steps.instructions:
Confirm that the installed circuit, flow sensor, expiratory components, and test lung match the selected Adult/Pediatric or Neonatal patient group.

Check whether the issue began after:

A circuit replacement
A patient-group change
A configuration change
Installation of a humidifier or accessory
Preventive maintenance or cleaning

Correct any mismatch and repeat the preoperational test.

Expected outcome: The physical circuit and configured patient group agree.

If correcting the configuration resolves the alarm, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 9. Review the High Pressure Alarm Limit and Plimit
steps.instructions:
Compare the high Pressure alarm limit with the selected ventilation settings and observed test-lung pressures.

Do not simply raise the alarm limit to silence an unexplained alarm. Confirm with respiratory therapy that the limit is clinically appropriate.

On the HAMILTON-C6, the high Pressure alarm limit and Plimit are linked; the high Pressure alarm limit is maintained 10 cmH₂O above Plimit.

If the alarm occurs only during the Sigh function, verify whether the message is High pressure during sigh. Hamilton recommends checking the circuit and airway for obstruction and considering disabling Sigh when clinically appropriate.

Expected outcome: Pressure settings and alarm limits are appropriate and are not creating a predictable nuisance alarm.

If an approved settings correction resolves the alarm, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 10. Test With a Known-Good Circuit and Test Lung
steps.instructions:
Install a complete known-good compatible breathing circuit, flow sensor, expiratory valve set, filters, and test lung.

Run the applicable preoperational check and ventilate the test lung using controlled settings. Observe:

Peak airway pressure
Pressure waveform
Delivered and exhaled tidal volume
PEEP stability
Alarm recurrence
Unusual turbine or valve sounds

Expected outcome: The ventilator operates normally with a verified external setup.

If the ventilator passes with the known-good setup, the original circuit or accessory assembly was the likely cause. Remove the defective component from use and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 11. Evaluate for a Ventilator-Side Fault
steps.instructions:
If the High pressure alarm continues with a verified circuit, flow sensor, expiratory valve, test lung, and appropriate settings, repeat the manufacturer-supported preoperational tests.

Watch for:

Expiratory-valve test failure
Flow-sensor calibration failure
Abnormal pressure readings at minimal settings
Pressure that remains elevated after the circuit is disconnected
Technical alarms
Ambient-state entry
Abnormal valve or turbine sounds

Hamilton states that the ventilator may enter the Ambient state when pressure remains substantially above the high Pressure alarm limit. Alternative ventilation is required if this occurs.

Expected outcome: A reproducible ventilator-side malfunction is identified without internal disassembly.

Do not proceed with internal pneumatic, valve, turbine, or pressure-transducer repair unless authorized, trained, and following current Hamilton service documentation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported repeated High pressure alarms on the Hamilton C6 during ventilation.
CCR.Cause: Testing found a saturated expiratory filter restricting exhaled flow and causing peak pressure to exceed the configured alarm limit.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced the expiratory filter, installed a verified breathing circuit, completed the preoperational check, and confirmed stable ventilation without recurring alarms.

helpfulDetails: High Pressure limit and Plimit settings
Expiratory valve set inspected or swapped

title: Hamilton C6 Ventilator - Disconnection or Low Pressure Alarm
description: Troubleshooting disconnection or low-pressure alarms caused by circuit leaks, loose connections, flow-sensor problems, accessories, test-lung setup, or incorrect alarm limits.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a persistent disconnection or low-pressure alarm while the HAMILTON-C6 is supporting a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team immediately. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Provide manual ventilation when clinically required and performed by qualified personnel. Confirm adequate ventilation and oxygenation using independent monitoring. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on a ventilator that may not be delivering the intended pressure or volume. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the affected ventilator has been removed from patient use.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Alarm Condition
steps.instructions: Review the active alarm message and alarm history. Determine whether the device reports: Disconnection; Pressure low; Expiratory minute volume low; Tidal volume low; Flow sensor error; Apnea; Multiple related alarms. Record whether the alarm occurs continuously, intermittently, during inspiration, or only with certain settings. The low-pressure alarm is generated when the ventilator does not reach the configured lower airway-pressure limit. Expected outcome: The specific alarm behavior and the conditions that trigger it are identified.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Patient Circuit for Complete Disconnection
steps.instructions: Trace the entire breathing circuit from the ventilator to the patient connection or test lung. Check: Inspiratory limb connection; Expiratory limb connection; Y-piece; Patient interface connection; Flow-sensor connections; Humidifier chamber connections; Nebulizer adapter; Water traps; Sampling adapters; Circuit extension tubing. Reseat every connection securely. Look for tubing that appears connected but is only partially inserted. Expected outcome: All circuit components are fully seated with no open or disconnected ports. If reconnecting the circuit resolves the alarm and the ventilator passes operational testing, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 4. Check for Cracks, Tears, or Loose Components
steps.instructions: Inspect the complete circuit for: Split tubing; Cracked connectors; Damaged Y-pieces; Loose swivel adapters; Missing caps; Open suction or sampling ports; Poorly seated humidifier chambers; Damaged test lungs; Loose exhalation components. Flex tubing gently while operating the ventilator on a test lung. An intermittent alarm may indicate a crack that opens when the circuit moves. Expected outcome: No visible or intermittent circuit leak is found. Replace any questionable disposable component before continuing.

steps.title: 5. Verify the Flow Sensor Installation
steps.instructions: Inspect the proximal flow sensor and its tubing or electrical connections, depending on the installed configuration. Confirm that: The sensor is installed in the correct orientation. Both flow-sensor lines or connectors are secure. The lines are not crossed, kinked, wet, blocked, or disconnected. The sensor body is not cracked or contaminated. The sensor matches the selected patient category. Any required calibration has been completed successfully. A disconnected or incorrectly installed flow sensor may produce inaccurate volume measurements and alarms that resemble a circuit disconnection. Expected outcome: The correct flow sensor is properly installed, recognized, and functioning. If the alarm clears after replacing or correctly installing the sensor, complete the required preoperational test and stop.

steps.title: 6. Inspect the Expiratory Valve Assembly
steps.instructions: Verify that the expiratory valve assembly is: Present; Correctly assembled; Fully seated; Clean and dry; Free of visible damage; Appropriate for the selected patient category. Check the expiratory membrane for incorrect positioning, wrinkles, tears, or contamination. Do not perform internal disassembly beyond routine user-removable components. Expected outcome: The expiratory valve assembly is properly installed and able to seal during inspiration.

steps.title: 7. Evaluate Humidifier and Accessory Connections
steps.instructions: Temporarily simplify the circuit when safe and appropriate for bench testing. Inspect or remove unnecessary accessories one at a time, including: Humidifier chamber; HME or HMEF; Nebulizer adapter; Closed-suction adapter; Capnography adapter; Circuit extension; Specialty connectors. Reconnect the ventilator to a verified test lung after each change. Additional components can affect resistance and the ventilator’s ability to identify a patient-side disconnection.
